rate-limiter.desc: Protect your APIs from abuse. Token bucket vs leaky bucket vs sliding window — know the tradeoffs.
rate-limiter.q: How will you solve this problem? Rate Limiter
rate-limiter.what:
Design a distributed rate limiter that limits API requests per user/IP. Support multiple rate limit rules (e.g. 100 req/min per user, 10 req/s per IP). The limiter should work across multiple API server instances.

Functional requirements

  • Allow/deny a request based on rate limit rules
  • Multiple rules: per-user, per-IP, per-endpoint
  • Return 429 with Retry-After header when limited
  • Config: rules stored in DB, hot-reloaded without restart
  • Admin API to update limits per customer tier

Non-functional / scale

  • Add < 1ms latency to each request
  • 10M req/s total throughput
  • Accurate across distributed servers
  • Rules updated within 30 seconds of config change
  • No single point of failure

Building blocks

  • Redis (atomic INCR + EXPIRE or Lua script)
  • Token bucket / sliding window log algorithm
  • Middleware in API gateway
  • Config service
  • Rule cache (local + Redis)
rate-limiter.why:
• Algorithm choice: Token Bucket is best for bursty traffic (allows bursts up to bucket size). Sliding Window Log is most accurate but memory-heavy. Fixed Window is simplest but has edge-case bursts at window boundaries.
  • Redis implementation: use INCR + EXPIRE for fixed window. For sliding window: store timestamps in a sorted set (ZADD), ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove old, ZCARD to count.
  • Distributed accuracy: all servers check the same Redis counter. Use a Lua script to make check-and-increment atomic (avoids race conditions).
  • Local cache: cache the rate limit decision locally for 100ms to reduce Redis calls. Slightly less accurate but hugely more scalable.

lru-cache.desc: Cache is at the heart of every scalable system. Understand eviction, consistency, and distribution.
lru-cache.q: How will you solve this problem? Distributed LRU Cache
lru-cache.what:
Design a distributed in-memory cache supporting GET/SET/DELETE with LRU eviction. The cache should be horizontally scalable (multiple nodes), support TTL per key, and handle node failures gracefully.

Functional requirements

  • GET key → value (or null)
  • SET key value [TTL]
  • DELETE key
  • LRU eviction when memory is full
  • Consistent hashing to shard across nodes

Non-functional / scale

  • 1M req/s across the cluster
  • Sub-millisecond read latency (P99 < 1ms)
  • 99.99% availability
  • Horizontal scalability: add nodes without downtime
  • Memory efficiency: no wasted space

Building blocks

  • Consistent hashing ring
  • Doubly linked list + HashMap (LRU internals)
  • Virtual nodes for load balancing
  • Gossip protocol for node membership
  • Replication factor for HA
lru-cache.why:
• LRU internals: HashMap for O(1) lookup + doubly-linked list for O(1) move-to-front and eviction of tail. This is the classic O(1) LRU.
  • Distribution: use consistent hashing — place nodes on a ring, route each key to the closest node clockwise. Minimizes re-distribution when nodes join/leave.
  • Replication: replicate each key to N successor nodes. On GET, read from 1 (faster) or 2 (more consistent). On write, write to all N replicas.
  • Failure handling: if a node goes down, consistent hashing automatically routes to the next node. Use heartbeats + gossip to detect failures within seconds.

pastebin.q: How will you solve this problem? Pastebin / Code Snippet Store
pastebin.why:
• Split content from metadata: store paste content in S3/blob storage (cheap, scalable), store metadata (id, owner, expiry, language) in a relational DB.
  • Unique key: 6-char Base62 gives 62^6 = 56B combinations. Generate randomly and check for collision (unlikely but handle it).
  • Expiry cleanup: use a TTL column + a background cron job that deletes expired pastes in batches. Redis can also handle TTL for the URL cache.
  • Read path: check Redis cache first → if miss, read metadata from DB + fetch content URL from S3 → return. Cache the paste for hot content.

url-shortener.desc: The "Hello World" of system design. Master this and you understand hashing, redirects, and scale basics.
url-shortener.q: How will you solve this problem? URL Shortener (TinyURL)
url-shortener.what:
Design a URL Shortening Service like TinyURL. Users paste a long URL and get a short code (e.g. tinyurl.com/abc123) that redirects to the original. The system must handle millions of redirects per day.

Functional requirements

  • Shorten a long URL to a unique short code
  • Redirect short URL to original URL (301/302)
  • Custom aliases (optional): user picks their own slug
  • Expiry: URLs can have a TTL after which they 404
  • Analytics: click count per short URL

Non-functional / scale

  • 100M URLs created per day, 10B redirects/day
  • Redirect latency < 10ms (P99)
  • High availability — 99.99% uptime
  • Short codes are unique and non-guessable
  • Storage: ~500 bytes per URL, estimate 5 years retention

Building blocks

  • Hash function (Base62)
  • Key-Value Store (Redis/DynamoDB)
  • CDN for redirect caching
  • Counter / UUID for unique ID
  • Rate limiter

kv-store.desc: The foundation of every data layer. Understand partitioning, replication, and consistency deeply.
kv-store.q: How will you solve this problem? Key-Value Store (Redis/DynamoDB Lite)
kv-store.what:
Design a distributed key-value store like DynamoDB or Cassandra. Support GET, PUT, DELETE operations. The store must be highly available, horizontally scalable, and support eventual consistency with tunable consistency levels.

Functional requirements

  • GET(key) → value
  • PUT(key, value) with optional TTL
  • DELETE(key)
  • Tunable consistency: ONE, QUORUM, ALL
  • Range scans on sorted keys (optional)

Non-functional / scale

  • 1M writes/s, 10M reads/s
  • P99 write latency < 10ms
  • Data replicated across 3 data centers
  • Auto-scale storage (petabyte scale)
  • Eventual consistency within 1 second

Building blocks

  • Consistent hashing for partitioning
  • Replication (3 replicas)
  • Vector clocks / Last-Write-Wins
  • Gossip protocol
  • Bloom filters
  • SSTable + LSM tree (write-optimized storage)

job-queue.desc: Async is everywhere — email sending, image resizing, report generation. Design the infrastructure for it.
job-queue.q: How would you solve this problem? Task Queue / Background Job System
job-queue.why:
• At-least-once delivery: use visibility timeout — when a worker picks a job, it becomes invisible for N seconds. If not ACKed in time, it re-appears for another worker. This guarantees delivery but requires idempotent job handlers.
  • Priority: use multiple queues (high/medium/low) or a sorted set in Redis (ZADD with priority score, ZPOPMIN to dequeue highest priority).
  • Retry with backoff: on failure, re-enqueue with delay = 2^attempt seconds. After max retries, move to dead-letter queue.
  • Scheduling: a separate scheduler process reads cron configs and enqueues jobs at the right time. Use distributed lock (Redis SETNX) to prevent duplicate scheduling across scheduler instances.

leaderboard.q: How will you solve this problem? Real-Time Leaderboard
leaderboard.what:
Design a real-time leaderboard for a gaming platform. Players submit scores. The system must show global top-100, a player's rank, and the 5 players above/below any player — all in real time.

Functional requirements

  • Submit score for a player (upsert — keep highest)
  • Get global top-100 leaderboard
  • Get rank of a specific player
  • Get players surrounding a player (±5 neighbours)
  • Leaderboard scoped by time window (daily/weekly/all-time)

Non-functional / scale

  • 10M players, 1M score updates/min
  • Rank query < 10ms
  • Top-100 updates reflected within 1 second
  • Multiple time windows maintained simultaneously
  • Globally distributed (low latency for all regions)

Building blocks

  • Redis Sorted Set (ZADD, ZRANK, ZRANGE)
  • Time-window sharding (separate sorted sets)
  • Write-through cache
  • Read replica for analytics
  • Pub/Sub for real-time push
leaderboard.why:
• Redis Sorted Set is the perfect data structure: ZADD O(log N) to insert/update, ZRANK O(log N) to get rank, ZRANGE O(log N + K) to get top-K. All the operations you need.
  • Time windows: maintain separate sorted sets per window (leaderboard:daily:2024-01-15, leaderboard:weekly:2024-W03, leaderboard:alltime). Use expiry on daily/weekly sets.
  • Score upsert: ZADD with NX flag only sets if not exists; without it, it always updates. To keep the highest score only: use a Lua script to check current score before updating.
  • Surrounding players: ZREVRANK to find player rank R, then ZREVRANGE R-5 to R+5 to get neighbours.

notification.q: How will you solve this problem? Notification System
notification.why:
• Architecture: producer → Kafka topic → consumer workers per channel (push, email, SMS). Each worker pulls from its topic and calls the appropriate provider.
  • Priority queues: use separate Kafka partitions or queues per priority. Critical notifications bypass the queue and are sent synchronously.
  • Provider failover: if FCM fails, retry with exponential backoff. After N failures, switch to backup provider (OneSignal). Track provider health.
  • Deduplication: before sending, check a Redis set with key = hash(userId + notificationType + content). If key exists, skip. Set TTL to 24h.

search-autocomplete.q: How will you solve this problem? Search Autocomplete / Typeahead
search-autocomplete.what:
Design a search autocomplete system that returns top-5 suggestions as the user types. Suggestions are ranked by search frequency. The system must handle billions of searches and update suggestions based on trending queries.

Functional requirements

  • Return top-5 completions for a prefix in < 100ms
  • Rank suggestions by search frequency (global + personalized)
  • Update frequency counts in near real-time (within 1 hour)
  • Support multiple languages and locales
  • Filter out adult/blocked content

Non-functional / scale

  • 10B searches/day, 12M queries/s peak for autocomplete
  • P99 latency < 50ms
  • Suggestions refreshed every 1 hour from search logs
  • 99.99% availability
  • Horizontally scalable

Building blocks

  • Trie (prefix tree) or prefix hash in Redis
  • Aggregation pipeline (Kafka + Flink/Spark)
  • CDN caching for common prefixes
  • Distributed Trie with sharding by prefix
  • Top-K algorithm (min-heap per node)
search-autocomplete.why:
• Data structure: Trie where each node stores top-K suggestions with their frequencies (not full trie traversal — precompute at each node). This makes reads O(length of prefix).
  • Scale: shard the trie by first character (26 shards). Each shard is a separate service. Route queries to the correct shard.
  • Update pipeline: search events → Kafka → Flink computes frequency over 1h windows → updates trie. Don't update trie on every search (too slow) — batch updates hourly.
  • CDN caching: most autocomplete queries are for common prefixes ("the", "how", "what"). Cache top prefixes at CDN edge nodes. Cache invalidation on hourly trie refresh.

web-crawler.desc: Google indexes the entire web — how? Distributed crawling, URL deduplication, and politeness rules.
web-crawler.q: How will you solve this problem? Web Crawler
web-crawler.what:
Design a distributed web crawler that crawls billions of web pages. The crawler should discover new URLs, avoid crawling the same URL twice, respect robots.txt and crawl-delay, and store crawled content for downstream indexing.

Functional requirements

  • Seed with initial URLs, discover new URLs from page links
  • Avoid duplicate URL crawling (deduplication)
  • Respect robots.txt and crawl-delay per domain
  • Prioritize URLs by PageRank / freshness
  • Store HTML content + metadata for indexing

Non-functional / scale

  • Crawl 1B pages/day (11K pages/sec)
  • URL frontier holds 100M pending URLs
  • Detect and handle duplicate content (near-duplicate)
  • Respect politeness: max 1 req/s per domain
  • Fault-tolerant: resume after worker crash

Building blocks

  • URL Frontier (priority queue)
  • DNS resolver cache
  • Bloom filter for URL deduplication
  • Content store (S3)
  • robots.txt cache
  • Consistent hashing for URL-to-worker assignment
web-crawler.why:
• URL deduplication: Bloom filter to quickly check if URL was seen (false positives OK — we just skip some URLs). Back it with a persistent hash set in DB for accuracy.
  • Politeness: assign URLs to workers by domain hash — same domain always goes to the same worker. Each worker maintains per-domain last-crawl timestamp and enforces crawl-delay.
  • URL frontier: priority queue with two tiers — front queue (prioritized by PageRank/freshness) and back queue (per-domain FIFO). Selector picks from front queues and routes to back queues respecting politeness.
  • Duplicate content: use SimHash (locality-sensitive hashing) to detect near-duplicate pages. If SimHash is within Hamming distance 3 of an existing page, skip or de-prioritize.

twitter.desc: The classic. Fan-out on write vs read, celebrity problem, timeline generation at scale.
twitter.q: How would you solve this problem? Twitter / Social Media Feed
twitter.why:
• Fan-out on write (push): when user A tweets, push to all followers' timeline caches immediately. Read is O(1). Problem: 100M follower celebrity → 100M cache writes.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): on timeline request, fetch tweets from all followees and merge. Problem: if you follow 1000 people, that's 1000 DB reads per timeline load.
  • Hybrid approach: fan-out on write for normal users (< 10K followers). Fan-out on read for celebrities. On timeline load, merge pre-built cache + real-time celebrity tweets.
  • Celebrity detection: flag users with > 1M followers. When they tweet, don't fan-out. Instead, store the tweet ID separately. On timeline read, inject celebrity tweets and re-rank.

uber.q: How will you solve this problem? Uber / Ride Sharing
uber.what:
Design Uber — riders request rides, drivers broadcast location, the system matches nearby drivers to riders, calculates routes and dynamic pricing, and tracks rides in real time.

Functional requirements

  • Driver location update (every 4 seconds)
  • Rider requests a ride with pickup + dropoff
  • Match rider to nearest available driver
  • Real-time ride tracking for both rider and driver
  • Dynamic pricing (surge) based on supply/demand
  • Trip history and receipts

Non-functional / scale

  • 5M drivers online simultaneously
  • Location update: 5M updates/20s = 250K writes/s
  • Driver matching: < 1 second
  • Location accuracy: 10-meter precision
  • Globally distributed, city-by-city operation

Building blocks

  • Geospatial index (QuadTree / S2 / H3 cells)
  • Location store (Redis with geo commands)
  • Matching service (proximity search)
  • WebSocket / SSE for real-time tracking
  • Pricing engine
  • Trip state machine
uber.why:
• Location storage: use Redis GEOADD to store driver locations. GEORADIUS finds all drivers within X km of a pickup point in O(N+log M) time.
  • Geospatial indexing: divide map into grid cells (H3 hexagons or QuadTree). Index drivers by cell. On rider request, search the cell and adjacent cells for available drivers.
  • Matching: find top-10 nearest drivers, rank by ETA (not raw distance — account for traffic). Offer trip to #1 driver, if declined in 10s move to #2, etc.
  • Surge pricing: track ride request rate vs driver supply ratio per cell in real-time. Surge multiplier = f(demand/supply). Update every 1-2 minutes.
  • Real-time tracking: driver app sends location every 4s over WebSocket. Server fans out to rider's WebSocket connection. Use a routing layer (Redis pub/sub) to connect driver to rider channel.

whatsapp.q: How will you solve this problem? WhatsApp / Messaging App
whatsapp.why:
• Connection: each device maintains a persistent WebSocket to a chat server. A routing service maps userId → server. When server A needs to deliver to a user on server B, it routes via inter-server messaging.
  • Offline delivery: if recipient is offline, store message in their inbox queue (Cassandra or Redis). On reconnect, client syncs from last seen message ID.
  • Group delivery: when sending to a group of 256, fan out to all 256 members' inboxes. The sender only sends once; the server handles fan-out. For very large groups (broadcast channels), use a different model.
  • Delivery receipts: ✓ when stored on server, ✓✓ when delivered to device (device ACKs), blue ✓✓ when app marks as read and sends read receipt to server.

instagram.q: How will you solve this problem? Instagram / Photo Sharing

ticketmaster.desc: Concurrency, seat locking, payment failures — how do you ensure two people never book the same seat?
ticketmaster.q: How would you solve this problem? Ticket Booking System (BookMyShow)
ticketmaster.what:
Design a ticket booking platform like BookMyShow. Users browse events, select seats, hold them temporarily, and complete payment. The system must prevent double-booking under high concurrency (e.g. Taylor Swift tickets going on sale).

Functional requirements

  • Browse events by city/date/venue
  • View seat map with availability
  • Hold selected seats for 10 minutes during checkout
  • Complete booking after payment
  • Cancel booking, release seats
  • Waiting list for sold-out events

Non-functional / scale

  • Millions of concurrent users during popular event sales
  • Zero double bookings
  • Seat hold expiry exactly at 10 minutes
  • Payment failure must release held seats
  • Read-heavy: seat map viewed 100x per booking

Building blocks

  • Distributed lock (Redis SETNX) for seat holding
  • Pessimistic locking on seat row in DB
  • Event queue for high-demand sale fairness
  • Payment service integration
  • Virtual waiting room
  • Seat map cache
ticketmaster.why:
• Seat holding: when user selects seats, acquire distributed lock per seat (Redis SET seat:{id}:hold {userId} NX EX 600). This prevents two users from holding the same seat.
  • On payment success: mark seat as BOOKED in DB, release the hold key. On failure or timeout: delete the lock key, seat becomes available again.
  • High-demand sales: implement a virtual waiting room. Users enter a queue, are admitted N at a time. This prevents server overload and ensures fairness (FIFO).
  • Double-booking prevention: even with distributed locks, use DB-level unique constraint on (event_id, seat_id, status=BOOKED) as the final safety net. Optimistic locking with version column on seat row as additional guard.

distributed-id.desc: Every distributed system needs unique IDs. Understand the snowflake design and its tradeoffs.
distributed-id.q: How would you solve this problem? Distributed ID Generator (Snowflake)

payment-system.q: How will you solve this problem? Payment Processing System
payment-system.what:
Design a payment processing system like Stripe or PayPal. Users link payment methods, initiate payments, and the system processes them through payment providers, handles retries, prevents double-charges, and reconciles with bank statements.

Functional requirements

  • Add and manage payment methods (card tokenization)
  • Initiate payment: debit source, credit destination
  • Idempotent payment API (retry-safe)
  • Handle async payment provider responses (webhooks)
  • Refunds: full and partial
  • Reconciliation: match payments to bank statements

Non-functional / scale

  • Exactly-once payment processing (no double charges)
  • P99 payment initiation < 2 seconds
  • Async provider responses within 30 seconds
  • PCI-DSS compliant card storage
  • Audit trail for every state transition
  • 99.99% availability

Building blocks

  • Idempotency key store (Redis)
  • Payment state machine (pending → processing → completed/failed)
  • Outbox pattern for reliable webhook handling
  • Card tokenization (via Vault/PCI proxy)
  • Ledger (append-only double-entry accounting)
  • Reconciliation service

google-drive.q: How will you solve this problem? Google Drive / File Storage
google-drive.why:
• Chunked upload: split file into 5MB chunks. Upload each chunk independently (parallel). Server tracks which chunks are received. On last chunk, assemble file. Supports resume on failure.
  • Deduplication: hash each chunk (SHA-256). Store chunks by hash — if two files share a chunk, store it once. This is block-level deduplication.
  • Delta sync: on file change, compute diff at chunk level. Only upload changed chunks. For a 1GB file with a 1KB edit, only upload the one changed 5MB chunk.
  • Conflict resolution: track client version ID. On sync, if server version != client base version, it's a conflict. Auto-merge if possible (text), else create conflict copy ("File (Conflicted copy 2024-01-15)").

kafka-design.desc: Kafka is the backbone of modern data engineering. Understand partitions, replication, and consumer groups.
kafka-design.q: How will you solve this problem? Distributed Message Queue (Kafka-like)

live-streaming.q: How would you solve this problem? Live Video Streaming (Twitch-like)
live-streaming.what:
Design a live video streaming platform like Twitch. Streamers broadcast live video, viewers watch with low latency. Support millions of concurrent viewers per stream, chat, stream recording, and VOD playback after stream ends.

Functional requirements

  • Streamer ingests video via RTMP
  • Transcoding to multiple quality levels (1080p/720p/480p/360p)
  • Viewers watch via HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate
  • Live chat alongside stream
  • DVR: pause and rewind up to 30 minutes into the past
  • Recording: save stream as VOD automatically

Non-functional / scale

  • 10K concurrent live streams
  • Each stream: up to 10M concurrent viewers
  • Glass-to-glass latency < 10 seconds (HLS), < 2 seconds (LL-HLS)
  • Transcoding: start within 5 seconds of stream start
  • 99.9% uptime for active streams

Building blocks

  • RTMP ingest servers
  • Real-time transcoder (FFmpeg workers)
  • HLS segmenter (2-4 second segments)
  • Origin + Edge CDN
  • Manifest server
  • Chat service (WebSocket)
  • Stream recording to S3
live-streaming.why:
• Ingest: streamer sends RTMP to nearest ingest point. DNS-based routing or Anycast routes to the closest server. Ingest server forwards stream to transcoder cluster.
  • Transcoding: GPU-accelerated FFmpeg workers transcode to multiple bitrates in real time. Each output segment (2-4s of video) is immediately available for viewers.
  • Distribution: HLS segments pushed to CDN origin, CDN edge nodes cache and serve to viewers. Viewers request manifest → get segment URLs → download segments → play.
  • Latency: standard HLS has 20-30s latency (6-10 segments × 3s). Low-Latency HLS reduces to 2-4s by using partial segments and HTTP/2 push. Tradeoff: more CDN pressure.
  • Chat: WebSocket chat service separate from video. Messages broadcast to all viewers of a stream. At 100K concurrent chatters, fan-out becomes expensive — use pub/sub (Redis) per stream channel.

youtube.q: How will you solve this problem? YouTube / Video Platform
youtube.what:
Design YouTube — users upload videos, which are transcoded to multiple resolutions and served globally via CDN. Design the upload pipeline, transcoding system, recommendation engine, and real-time view count.

Functional requirements

  • Video upload (up to 128GB)
  • Transcode to 240p/360p/480p/720p/1080p/4K + audio tracks
  • Adaptive bitrate streaming (ABR)
  • Search by title, description, channel
  • Recommendations: homepage, "Up Next" sidebar
  • Comments, likes, subscriptions, notifications
  • Real-time view count (eventually consistent ok)

Non-functional / scale

  • 500 hours of video uploaded every minute
  • 1B hours watched daily
  • Upload processing complete within 30 minutes
  • P99 video start time < 2 seconds
  • CDN hit ratio > 99%
  • View count accurate within 5% in real time

Building blocks

  • Chunked upload + resumable upload API
  • Transcoding pipeline (distributed FFmpeg workers)
  • Blob storage for raw + processed video
  • Global CDN (multi-tier)
  • Search index (Elasticsearch)
  • ML recommendation engine (embeddings + collaborative filtering)
  • Real-time analytics pipeline (Kafka + Flink)
  • View count (Redis HyperLogLog + batch reconciliation)

google-maps.q: How would you solve this problem? Google Maps / Navigation
google-maps.what:
Design Google Maps — serve map tiles, calculate routes between locations, show real-time traffic, provide ETA estimates, and update the road network from user data.

Functional requirements

  • Serve map tiles at any zoom level
  • Route calculation: fastest/shortest between two points
  • Turn-by-turn navigation with re-routing
  • Real-time traffic: display congestion, ETA impact
  • Search: find places by name or category
  • User contributions: report accidents, road closures

Non-functional / scale

  • 1B daily active users
  • Map tile: serve 10B tile requests/day, < 50ms
  • Route calculation < 1 second for cross-city
  • < 3 seconds cross-country
  • Traffic data updated every 60 seconds
  • Map data: 100TB+ compressed

Building blocks

  • Graph database for road network (nodes=intersections, edges=roads)
  • Dijkstra / A* / Contraction Hierarchies for routing
  • Quadtree for spatial indexing
  • Map tile precomputation + CDN
  • Traffic ingestion pipeline (GPS probes)
  • ETA model (ML)
  • Place index (Elasticsearch)
google-maps.why:
• Road network graph: nodes are intersections, edges are road segments with weight = travel time (dynamic, based on traffic). Store as adjacency list. Global graph has billions of nodes.
  • Routing algorithm: plain Dijkstra is too slow for global scale. Use Contraction Hierarchies (CH): preprocess graph by adding "shortcut" edges. Reduces query time from minutes to milliseconds for cross-country routes.
  • Map tiles: precompute PNG/vector tiles for each zoom level (0-22). Store in S3, serve via CDN. Tile = quadkey (Morton code encoding lat/lng). Only render changed tiles on map update.
  • Real-time traffic: collect GPS pings from user devices (anonymized). Aggregate speed per road segment — low speed = congestion. Weight edges in graph with real-time speed. Update routing weights every 60s.
  • ETA: use ML model (features: distance, road type, time of day, day of week, live traffic) rather than pure graph traversal. Historical data trains the model.

uber-advanced.q: How would you solve this problem? Uber Marketplace (Supply-Demand)
uber-advanced.what:
Design the Uber dispatch and pricing marketplace at production scale. Focus on the matching algorithm, real-time ETA prediction, surge pricing computation, driver supply management, and global fleet orchestration.

Functional requirements

  • Real-time driver ETA prediction (traffic-aware)
  • Surge pricing: compute multiplier per geographic cell
  • Optimal driver dispatch (minimize rider wait time globally)
  • Driver incentive programs (hourly guarantees)
  • Marketplace health: prevent supply-demand imbalance
  • Multi-product: UberX, Uber Black, Uber Pool

Non-functional / scale

  • 5M concurrent drivers, 100M daily trips
  • Matching decision < 500ms
  • ETA accurate to ±30 seconds
  • Surge pricing recalculated every 2 minutes per H3 cell
  • Global operation (50+ countries)
  • Pricing engine handles 1M price calculations/second

Building blocks

  • H3 geospatial hexagonal grid
  • ETA ML model (graph + traffic + time features)
  • Matching optimization (bipartite graph matching)
  • Supply-demand forecasting (LSTM)
  • Surge multiplier compute pipeline
  • Driver state machine
  • Incentive engine
uber-advanced.why:
• H3 cells: divide the world into hexagonal cells at multiple resolutions. Resolution 8 = ~0.74 km² per cell. Aggregate supply (drivers) and demand (requests) per cell. Surge is per-cell.
  • Matching: model as bipartite graph matching — riders on left, drivers on right, edge weight = ETA. Find minimum weight matching (Hungarian algorithm). In practice, use greedy approximation for real-time.
  • ETA model: features include distance, turn count, road types, time-of-day, real-time traffic speed per segment. Trained on historical trip data. Served from a low-latency ML inference server.
  • Surge pricing: multiplier = f(demand_rate / supply_rate) for the cell. Smooth changes over time (no sudden 5x jumps). Caps at regulatory limits per city. Communicate to driver and rider before trip.
  • Supply forecasting: LSTM model predicts driver supply 30-60 mins in future. Trigger incentives ("earn $50 bonus if you drive in downtown for next hour") before anticipated shortage.

facebook-messenger.q: How will you solve this problem? Facebook Messenger (At Scale)
facebook-messenger.what:
Design Facebook Messenger — 1:1 and group messaging for 1B users, multi-device sync (all your devices see the same messages), end-to-end encryption, read receipts, message reactions, and disappearing messages.

Functional requirements

  • 1:1 and group messaging (up to 150 members)
  • Multi-device sync: messages appear on all devices
  • E2E encryption (Signal protocol)
  • Read receipts and typing indicators
  • Message reactions (emoji)
  • Disappearing messages (timed expiry)
  • Message search within conversation

Non-functional / scale

  • 1B users, 10B messages/day
  • 100M concurrent WebSocket connections
  • Message delivery < 500ms (both online)
  • Multi-device sync within 2 seconds
  • Messages stored encrypted at rest
  • 99.999% availability for core messaging

Building blocks

  • Connection service (WebSocket farm)
  • Inbox service (per-user message store)
  • Fan-out service (group delivery)
  • Key server (public key distribution for E2EE)
  • Sync cursor per device
  • Presence aggregation service
  • Search index (encrypted index)
facebook-messenger.why:
• 100M WebSockets: each WebSocket server holds 50K connections. Need 2000 servers. Use consistent hashing to route each user to their WebSocket server. Store mapping in Redis.
  • Multi-device sync: every message has a monotonically increasing ID per conversation. Each device tracks its last-seen ID. On reconnect, device requests messages since last-seen ID.
  • E2EE: uses Signal protocol (X3DH key exchange + Double Ratchet). Each device has a public key registered on the key server. Sender fetches recipient's public key, encrypts message client-side. Server never sees plaintext.
  • Group messaging at scale: for 150-member groups, fan-out to each member's inbox. For very large groups (Messenger Rooms), use a different "broadcast" model — members pull from a shared conversation log.
  • Typing indicators: ephemeral — not stored. Sender publishes to a pub/sub channel. Recipient's WebSocket server is subscribed. Delivered via WebSocket push. TTL = 5 seconds (stop indicator if no new event).

netflix.q: How will you solve this problem? Netflix / Video Streaming Platform
netflix.what:
Design Netflix — content ingestion and encoding pipeline, global CDN distribution, personalized recommendations, A/B testing infrastructure, and the resilience patterns (circuit breakers, chaos monkey) that keep it running.

Functional requirements

  • Content ingestion: studios upload master files
  • Encode to 1000+ output profiles (device + quality combos)
  • Personalized homepage ranked by predicted enjoyment
  • Continue watching: resume from last position
  • Downloads for offline viewing
  • A/B test different artwork, recommendations, UI

Non-functional / scale

  • 220M subscribers, 1B+ hours streamed/day
  • Content available globally with < 50ms start time
  • Supports 2000+ device types
  • CDN caches 90%+ of traffic at edge
  • Zero downtime deployments
  • Chaos engineering: system survives random instance failures

Building blocks

  • Open Connect CDN (Netflix-owned PoPs)
  • Encoding pipeline (Unified Streaming Platform)
  • Recommendation system (collaborative filtering + deep learning)
  • Eventing backbone (Kafka)
  • Feature store for ML
  • Zuul API gateway
  • Hystrix circuit breaker
  • Chaos Monkey
netflix.why:
• Encoding at scale: a single film generates 1200+ output files (every combination of resolution, bitrate, codec, HDR, audio language). Parallel encode farm. Each shot independently encodable — "per-title encoding" optimizes bitrate for content complexity.
  • Open Connect: Netflix ships servers to ISPs. ISPs install them inside their network. Popular content is cached at the ISP level. This dramatically reduces transit costs and latency. Cache fill = nightly from Netflix origin.
  • Recommendations: two-stage architecture. Offline: train models on viewing history (matrix factorization + deep learning). Online: low-latency serving retrieves precomputed recommendations from Redis, then re-ranks using real-time context.
  • Resilience: Netflix pioneered chaos engineering — randomly terminate production instances to ensure the system self-heals. Hystrix circuit breaker: if a downstream service fails, return cached/default response rather than propagating failure.
  • A/B testing: every user is in dozens of experiments simultaneously. Feature flags control which variant each user sees. Experiment service tracks which group, logs interactions to Kafka, analyzes with Spark.

google-search.q: How will you solve this problem? Google Search Engine
google-search.what:
Design Google Search — a web-scale search engine that crawls the internet, builds an inverted index, computes PageRank, understands natural language queries, and returns ranked results in < 500ms.

Functional requirements

  • Crawl web pages continuously
  • Build and update inverted index
  • Compute and update PageRank
  • Query understanding: spelling correction, synonym expansion, entity recognition
  • Ranking: relevance score from 200+ signals
  • Results: 10 blue links + featured snippets + knowledge panel
  • Personalization: adjust results based on location, history

Non-functional / scale

  • Index 100B+ web pages
  • Query throughput: 100K QPS
  • Result latency < 500ms P99
  • Index freshness: major pages re-indexed within hours
  • New pages discovered within 24 hours of publication
  • Ranking models update continuously

Building blocks

  • Distributed web crawler
  • Document store (raw + parsed HTML)
  • Inverted index (distributed, sharded by term)
  • PageRank computation (distributed graph processing)
  • Query parser + NLU service
  • Ranking service (ML model serving)
  • Snippet generator
  • Cache for hot queries
google-search.why:
• Inverted index: maps term → list of (docId, tf-idf score, positions). Index is sharded by term across thousands of machines. A query hits multiple shards in parallel, results merged.
  • Two-phase retrieval: Phase 1 (recall) — retrieve top-1000 candidate docs per query term using BM25 from inverted index shards. Phase 2 (ranking) — run 200+ signal ranking model on candidates to get final top-10.
  • PageRank: solve the eigenvector equation iteratively using distributed graph processing (like Pregel/Spark GraphX). Run on the web graph nightly. Billions of nodes.
  • Query latency budget: 500ms total. Roughly: query parsing 10ms + distributed index lookup 100ms + ranking 200ms + snippet generation 100ms + network 90ms. Each step has strict SLA.
  • Index freshness: full crawl takes months. Use a real-time crawl layer that prioritizes high-value pages (news, popular sites) for re-crawl every few hours. Update index incrementally.

discord.q: How will you solve this problem? Discord (Gaming Chat at Scale)
discord.why:
• Message storage: Discord uses Cassandra partitioned by channel_id, with clustering key message_id (snowflake). This gives fast time-range queries per channel. They stored trillions of messages in Cassandra (and later moved to ScyllaDB).
  • Presence at scale: 500M users × online/offline events = massive update volume. Batch presence updates, fan out to interested parties (users sharing a guild). Use a pub/sub system — "user X came online" → notify all guild members of user X.
  • Voice SFU: each participant sends audio/video once to the SFU. SFU forwards to all other participants (selectively). Better than mesh (P2P, doesn't scale) or MCU (transcodes, CPU-heavy). WebRTC for transport.
  • Permission model: users have roles, roles have permissions, permissions are per-channel. Cache the resolved permission bitfield per (user, channel) in Redis. Invalidate on role change.
  • Large server fan-out: a message in a 500K-member Discord server must fan out to potentially 50K online users. Use a hierarchical fan-out: message → regional fan-out servers → per-user WebSocket servers → clients.

ads-system.desc: Real-time bidding, targeting, budget pacing, click fraud detection — ads fund the internet.
ads-system.q: How will you solve this problem? Ad Serving System (Google Ads)
ads-system.what:
Design a digital advertising platform like Google Ads. Advertisers create campaigns with budgets and targeting criteria. When a user makes a query/visits a page, the system runs a real-time auction to select the winning ad in < 10ms.

Functional requirements

  • Advertiser creates campaigns with budget, bid, targeting (keywords, demographics, geo)
  • Real-time auction: when user triggers ad opportunity, run auction among eligible ads
  • Budget pacing: spread spend evenly throughout day
  • Click tracking: record and bill per click (CPC model)
  • Conversion tracking: did user buy after seeing ad?
  • Reporting: impressions, clicks, CTR, spend, ROAS

Non-functional / scale

  • 100B ad auctions/day = 1.15M auctions/second
  • Auction latency < 10ms P99
  • Budget pacing accuracy: ±10% of daily budget
  • Click fraud detection in real time
  • Billing accuracy: no overcharging
  • Reporting data available with < 30 min lag

Building blocks

  • Ad index (eligible ads per targeting criteria)
  • Real-time bidding engine
  • Budget tracker (distributed counter)
  • Pacing algorithm
  • Click and impression log pipeline (Kafka)
  • Fraud detection (ML model)
  • Billing reconciliation
  • Reporting pipeline (Spark)
ads-system.why:
• Ad retrieval: given a query/page context, retrieve eligible ads in < 5ms. Use an inverted index of (keyword → ad IDs). Intersection of targeting criteria narrows candidates.
  • Auction (Generalized Second Price): rank ads by eCPM = bid × predicted CTR. Winner pays min price to maintain rank over #2 (not their own bid). Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism.
  • Budget pacing: naively spending budget as fast as possible burns daily budget in minutes. Use a token bucket per campaign — refill tokens at rate = daily_budget / seconds_in_day. Auction only proceeds if tokens available.
  • Distributed budget counter: all auction servers need to read/write the same budget. Use Redis with atomic DECRBY. Risk: Redis latency adds to auction time. Solution: each auction server maintains a local budget estimate, syncs with Redis every 100ms.
  • Click fraud: ML model scores each click on features: IP reputation, click velocity, user agent, device fingerprint, time-of-click patterns. Block fraudulent clicks before billing advertiser.

typeahead-ml.desc: The infrastructure behind every ML-powered product: features, training, serving, and monitoring.
typeahead-ml.q: How will you solve this problem? ML Feature Store & Model Serving
typeahead-ml.what:
Design a ML Feature Store and Model Serving platform. Data scientists define features, the platform computes them from raw data (batch + streaming), stores point-in-time correct feature values, serves them with < 10ms latency at inference time, and monitors model health in production.

Functional requirements

  • Define feature groups with transformation logic
  • Batch computation of features from historical data
  • Streaming computation of real-time features
  • Point-in-time correct joins for training data generation
  • Feature serving: fetch features by entity ID in < 10ms
  • Model registry: version, deploy, rollback models
  • A/B testing: shadow mode, canary, champion-challenger
  • Model monitoring: data drift, prediction distribution, business metrics

Non-functional / scale

  • 10K feature definitions, 1B entities
  • Batch compute: run 10K feature pipelines nightly
  • Real-time features: sub-second freshness
  • Serving: 1M feature lookups/second at < 10ms P99
  • Training: generate training dataset of 100B rows
  • Monitoring: alert on drift within 30 minutes

Building blocks

  • Feature registry (metadata store)
  • Batch compute (Spark)
  • Stream compute (Flink/Kafka Streams)
  • Online store (Redis for serving)
  • Offline store (Hive/Parquet for training)
  • Model registry (MLflow/Vertex)
  • A/B experiment framework
  • Data drift detector
  • Shadow scoring pipeline
typeahead-ml.why:
• Dual store architecture: offline store (S3/Hive, columnar, for training) + online store (Redis, row-oriented, for inference). Batch pipeline writes to both. Stream pipeline updates online store in real time.
  • Point-in-time correct joins: when generating training data, join features using the timestamp when the label event occurred — not current feature values. This prevents data leakage (using future information to predict the past).
  • Feature freshness tiers: static features (user age, signup date) updated daily. Engagement features (last 7-day clicks) updated hourly. Real-time features (current session activity) updated sub-second via stream.
  • Model serving: model loaded in memory in serving containers. Feature lookup from Redis, model inference (< 5ms for a shallow model, 50ms for deep neural net), return prediction. Autoscale based on QPS.
  • Monitoring: compare live prediction score distribution vs training distribution (KL divergence). Compare live feature distributions vs training. Alert if drift exceeds threshold. Track business metrics (CTR, conversion rate) downstream.

global-database.q: How will you solve this problem? Globally Distributed Database (Spanner-like)
global-database.why:
• TrueTime: Spanner's secret weapon. Google's servers have GPS receivers and atomic clocks. TrueTime API returns [earliest, latest] interval containing true current time (uncertainty ~1-7ms). Spanner waits out this uncertainty before committing — guarantees no future transaction can get a lower timestamp.
  • Paxos per shard: each shard (tablet) is replicated across 5 data centers via Paxos. Paxos leader handles reads/writes. Leader election is automatic. Writes need majority quorum (3/5).
  • Cross-shard transactions: use 2-Phase Commit coordinated by a transaction manager. 2PC is normally slow and blocks on failure — Spanner uses Paxos per participant to make each 2PC participant fault-tolerant.
  • MVCC: every write is tagged with a commit timestamp. Reads at timestamp T see the latest version of each row with commit_ts ≤ T. No read-write conflicts — reads never block writes.
  • External consistency means: if transaction T2 starts after T1 commits (in wall-clock time), T2 must see T1's writes. TrueTime guarantees this by ensuring commit timestamp of T1 < start timestamp of T2.
